title: Blog 1
content:
Least Privilege Security with Amazon EKS Pod Identity & Session Policies Introduction & Context When running containerized workloads on Kubernetes with Amazon EKS, assigning AWS permissions to pods has always been a critical architectural decision. Historically, teams relied on IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA), which required setting up an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider and complex trust policies per cluster.
AWS recently introduced Amazon EKS Pod Identity, streamlining role assumption down to an EKS add-on agent. Furthermore, the addition of Session Policies allows engineers to dynamically narrow IAM permissions for specific pods without needing to create new IAM roles for every microservice.
Why Are Session Policies a Game-Changer? In a multi-tenant or microservices Kubernetes cluster:
The IAM Role Explosion Problem: If Service A only needs read access to bucket-a and Service B only needs read access to bucket-b, engineers previously had to maintain two nearly identical IAM Roles. Quota Limitations: AWS accounts enforce limits on the number of IAM Roles per account (default: 1,000 roles). High-density clusters quickly approach this limit. Session Policy Intersection: With a Session Policy, the effective permissions are the mathematical intersection of the base IAM Role and the inline Session Policy: $$\text{Effective Permissions} = \text{IAM Role Permissions} \cap \text{Session Policy Permissions}$$
Important Rule: A session policy can only restrict or narrow permissions; it can never grant more access than the underlying IAM role permits.
Architecture & How It Works The Kubernetes Pod starts with an assigned ServiceAccount. The Amazon EKS Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet intercepts AWS STS calls from the AWS SDK inside the container. EKS requests temporary STS credentials from AWS IAM using the associated IAM Role and appends the configured Session Policy. The pod receives credentials valid strictly for its specific scoped operations. Hands-on Configuration Example 1. Define the Base IAM Role The base IAM Role (EKS-General-Storage-Role) permits broad S3 read operations:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } 2. Restrict per Pod via Session Policy When creating the EKS Pod Identity Association via the AWS CLI, provide a Session Policy that restricts the pod to only read from my-finance-reports-prod bucket:
aws eks create-pod-identity-association \ --cluster-name production-eks-cluster \ --namespace finance-apps \ --service-account finance-reporter \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/EKS-General-Storage-Role \ --client-token $(uuidgen) The inline session policy applied to this association:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-finance-reports-prod/*" } ] } Even though the base role allows reading all S3 buckets, this specific pod cannot read from any bucket other than my-finance-reports-prod.
Key Takeaways for DevOps Engineers Clean Governance: Manage a handful of generalized base roles while tailoring exact permissions per Kubernetes deployment. Simplified Cluster Provisioning: No need to configure an OIDC provider or manage complex IAM trust policies containing cluster OIDC issuer URLs. Audit Trail: AWS CloudTrail records show both the assumed role and the session name, ensuring complete traceability for security audits.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Blog 2
content:
High-Performance & Secure Static Web Hosting with S3 & CloudFront OAC The Dilemma: Fast, Cheap, but Is It Secure? Hosting single-page applications (React, Vue, Hugo, Next.js static exports) on Amazon S3 is a beloved design pattern due to its near-infinite scalability, 99.999999999% (11 9’s) data durability, and virtually negligible costs.
However, many beginner guides suggest checking “Static Website Hosting” on the S3 bucket and adding a public s3:GetObject bucket policy. This approach comes with severe downsides:
The S3 bucket URL is completely public and vulnerable to scrapers, DDoS, and hotlinking. AWS S3 direct endpoints do not natively support modern HTTPS certificates on custom domain names. Data Transfer Out (DTO) directly from S3 is more expensive than routing through the global Content Delivery Network (CDN). The Modern Standard: CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC) In 2022, AWS released Origin Access Control (OAC) to replace the legacy Origin Access Identity (OAI). OAC brings major improvements:
Supports all S3 regions, including newly added ones. Supports Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS). Supports dynamic HTTP PUT, DELETE methods if needed, alongside standard GET requests. [ User Browser ] | (HTTPS / HTTP3 - Worldwide Edge Locations) v [ Amazon CloudFront CDN ] | (Signed AWS SigV4 Request via OAC) v [ Private Amazon S3 Bucket ] (Block All Public Access: ON) Implementation Guide 1. Keep S3 Completely Private Turn on “Block all public access” on your S3 bucket. Do not enable “Static website hosting”. Keep it as a standard private storage bucket.
2. Create the CloudFront Distribution Set the Origin domain to your S3 bucket’s regional endpoint: your-bucket-name.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com. Under Origin access, select Origin access control settings (recommended) and click Create new OAC. Select Redirect HTTP to HTTPS in the default cache behavior. Set default root object to index.html. 3. Attach the S3 Bucket Policy CloudFront generates a tailored bucket policy. Apply this policy to your S3 bucket:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": { "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontServicePrincipalReadOnly", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::123456789012:distribution/EDFDVBD6EXAMPLE" } } } } Notice the crucial AWS:SourceArn condition key: It guarantees that only your specific CloudFront distribution can read objects from your bucket, preventing unauthorized distributions in other accounts from accessing your assets.
Performance & Cost Optimization Tips Leverage Cache-Control Headers:
Configure your build pipeline to upload static assets (like .js and .css files with content hashes) with long cache lifetimes: aws s3 cp ./build/static s3://your-bucket-name/static \ --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" Handle Single Page App Client-Side Routing:
Add a custom error response in CloudFront: Map HTTP 403 / 404 error codes to respond with /index.html and HTTP status 200, allowing React Router to handle page routes smoothly. Invalidate Only What Changed:
Avoid paying for excessive /* invalidations on busy repositories. Whenever possible, invalidate specific file paths (e.g., /index.html). Conclusion By combining Amazon S3 with CloudFront and Origin Access Control, you get an enterprise-grade web hosting setup that is blazing fast, strictly secured, and costs merely pennies per month.

title: Proposal
content:
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab research team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance microclimate weather data collection, visualization, and automated analytics. It supports up to 5 distributed weather stations with built-in scalability to 15 stations, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge nodes paired with ESP32 sensor modules to transmit telemetry over MQTT.
The platform leverages modern AWS Serverless services to provide real-time dashboarding, predictive analytics, and cost-optimized operations, secured with role-based access for lab researchers via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement The Current Challenge Existing research weather stations depend heavily on manual, on-site data extraction using SD cards. As the number of deployed nodes increases, this process quickly becomes labor-intensive and prone to data gaps. Moreover, third-party commercial IoT platforms charge high recurring subscription fees while offering rigid, black-box architectures unsuitable for customized academic research.
The Proposed Solution Our architecture implements an end-to-end cloud pipeline:
Ingestion: AWS IoT Core ingests real-time MQTT sensor telemetry securely with X.509 device certificates. Storage & Data Lake: Raw JSON readings are batched directly into an Amazon S3 Data Lake. ETL Transformation: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog schemas, and scheduled AWS Glue ETL jobs transform raw records into optimized columnar Apache Parquet files stored in an analytics bucket. Processing & API: AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway expose lightweight REST APIs for device management and historical queries. Frontend Application: An interactive Next.js web dashboard hosted on AWS Amplify provides live visualization, interactive charting, and device telemetry metrics. Authentication: Amazon Cognito handles user authentication, ensuring restricted access to authorized research personnel. Benefits & Return on Investment (ROI) Automation: Completely eliminates manual on-site data harvesting, saving dozens of research hours monthly. Cost Efficiency: Architecture costs only approximately $0.70 USD/month (~$8.40 USD/year) via AWS Free Tier and Serverless on-demand billing. Extensibility: Provides a solid, reusable dataset for future Machine Learning and AI climate forecasting models. 3. Solution Architecture The serverless platform architecture is divided into the Edge Ingestion Layer and the Cloud Processing Platform:
Key AWS Services Used: AWS IoT Core: Handles mutual TLS authentication and message brokering for MQTT sensor payloads. AWS Lambda: Serverless compute for lightweight API backends and event-triggered processing. Amazon API Gateway: Exposes secure REST endpoints with request validation and throttling. Amazon S3: Highly durable storage for raw JSON telemetry and processed Parquet analytical datasets. AWS Glue: Serverless data cataloging and PySpark ETL transformations. AWS Amplify: Full-stack hosting for the responsive Next.js web console. Amazon Cognito: User directory and JWT authorization for lab members. 4. Technical Implementation Phases Phase 1: Architecture Design & Hardware Prototyping (Month 0 - Pre-internship)
Researched ESP32 sensor pinouts, calibrated temperature/humidity/pressure sensors, and designed the AWS target architecture. Phase 2: Cost Modeling & Feasibility Validation (Month 1)
Modeled exact request quotas and data throughput using the AWS Pricing Calculator to confirm monthly costs stay below $1 USD. Phase 3: Core Service Provisioning & Pipeline Integration (Month 2)
Configured IoT Core rules, S3 storage buckets, Glue ETL scripts, and Lambda REST API endpoints using AWS CDK/CloudFormation. Phase 4: Dashboard Deployment, Field Testing & Optimization (Month 3)
Built the Next.js frontend, deployed on Amplify, completed end-to-end load testing, and calibrated edge Wi-Fi reconnection handling. 5. Timeline & Milestones Milestone 1: Edge firmware stabilized, sensor telemetry flowing reliably to AWS IoT Core. Milestone 2: S3 Data Lake and automated Glue ETL pipeline operational. Milestone 3: Amplify web dashboard connected with Cognito authentication and live charts. Milestone 4: Full stress testing and final documentation completed. 6. Budget Estimation Estimated monthly cost breakdown using the AWS Pricing Calculator:
Service Monthly Volume / Usage Estimated Monthly Cost AWS IoT Core 5 stations, ~45,000 MQTT messages/month $0.08 USD Amazon S3 6 GB storage, ~2,100 PUT/GET requests $0.15 USD AWS Lambda 1,000 invocations, 512 MB memory $0.00 USD (Free Tier) Amazon API Gateway 2,000 REST requests $0.01 USD AWS Glue 1 Crawler + 2 DPU-hours ETL batching $0.09 USD AWS Amplify Static hosting & Next.js SSR build/bandwidth $0.35 USD Data Transfer Out 1 GB egress bandwidth $0.02 USD Total Cloud Cost Estimated Total ~$0.70 USD / month Hardware investment: Existing lab equipment (ESP32, sensors, Raspberry Pi 5) valued at ~$265 USD was repurposed, incurring zero additional hardware expense.
7. Risk Assessment & Mitigation Intermittent Network Disconnectivity:
Risk: Edge stations may drop Wi-Fi connection during stormy weather.
Mitigation: Edge Raspberry Pi stores readings in a local SQLite buffer with Docker; cached payloads automatically sync to AWS IoT Core once network connectivity is restored. Sensor Drift & Hardware Failures:
Risk: Sensor corrosion or incorrect calibration values.
Mitigation: Sensor health heartbeat telemetry and spare sensor kits ready for immediate hot-swapping. Unexpected Cloud Billing Spikes:
Risk: Errant infinite loops or retry storms driving up serverless charges.
Mitigation: AWS Budgets with $2/month threshold alerts and hard concurrency limits set on Lambda functions. 8. Expected Outcomes & Project Impact Autonomous Operations: Continuous 24/7 climate monitoring without human intervention. Empirical Research Asset: High-fidelity, clean historical weather dataset ready for machine learning model training and academic publication.

title: Blog 3
content:
Building an Event-Driven Serverless Image Processing Pipeline with S3, Lambda & DynamoDB Problem Statement In virtually every modern web platform (e-commerce, social media, blogging), users upload high-resolution profile pictures or product photos. If our application attempts to resize and process these large images synchronously inside the main web server process:
Server threads get tied up waiting for heavy CPU-bound image transformations. User response times spike significantly, leading to poor user experience. Peak upload spikes can easily crash the web servers. The elegant, cloud-native solution is to decouple ingestion from processing using an asynchronous event-driven architecture.
Solution Architecture [ User Uploads Image ] | v [ Amazon S3 (Upload Bucket) ] | (s3:ObjectCreated:* Event) v [ AWS Lambda (Resizer Function) ] | | | (Save Thumbnail) | (Persist Metadata) v v [ Amazon S3 (Resized) ] [ Amazon DynamoDB ] The frontend application uploads the original image directly to an Amazon S3 Source Bucket (optionally using S3 Presigned URLs). Amazon S3 automatically fires an ObjectCreated event notification to an AWS Lambda function. AWS Lambda streams the original image, performs proportional resizing and optimization (using the Pillow or Sharp image library), and writes the resized image to a Target S3 Bucket. Simultaneously, Lambda saves the metadata record (original file size, thumbnail URL, timestamp, dimensions) into Amazon DynamoDB. Hands-on Implementation Details 1. Preventing the Infinite Loop Trap Critical Architectural Warning: Never configure an S3 event notification to trigger a Lambda function that writes back into the same bucket with the same prefix. Doing so will cause an infinite execution loop where the output triggers another execution, rapidly draining your AWS budget. Always use two distinct buckets (e.g. raw-images-bucket and processed-images-bucket) or strict prefix filtering (uploads/ vs thumbnails/).
2. The Python Lambda Handler Code Here is an idiomatic Python Lambda function using the Pillow library and AWS SDK (boto3):
import os import urllib.parse import boto3 from PIL import Image import io import time s3_client = boto3.client('s3') dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table(os.environ['METADATA_TABLE']) OUTPUT_BUCKET = os.environ['OUTPUT_BUCKET'] def lambda_handler(event, context): for record in event['Records']: source_bucket = record['s3']['bucket']['name'] key = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(record['s3']['object']['key']) # Download image into memory buffer response = s3_client.get_object(Bucket=source_bucket, Key=key) image_bytes = response['Body'].read() # Process thumbnail image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes)) image.thumbnail((300, 300)) buffer = io.BytesIO() image.save(buffer, 'JPEG', quality=85) buffer.seek(0) # Save thumbnail to output bucket output_key = f"thumbnails/{key}" s3_client.put_object( Bucket=OUTPUT_BUCKET, Key=output_key, Body=buffer, ContentType='image/jpeg' ) # Record metadata in DynamoDB table.put_item( Item={ 'image_id': key, 'timestamp': int(time.time()), 'source_bucket': source_bucket, 'thumbnail_key': output_key, 'width': image.width, 'height': image.height } ) return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': 'Image processed successfully'} Resilience & Production Considerations Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ):
Attach an Amazon SQS Dead-Letter Queue to the Lambda function. If a corrupted image file fails processing after standard retries, the failed event payload is captured in SQS for debugging rather than lost silently. Lambda Memory Configuration:
Because AWS Lambda scales CPU power proportionally to allocated memory, assigning 1,024 MB or 1,536 MB of RAM often makes image processing 3x faster, resulting in a lower net execution cost despite the higher per-second rate. Ephemeral Storage (/tmp):
For larger files (e.g., videos or massive raw camera formats), you can increase the /tmp scratch space up to 10 GB. Summary By adopting an event-driven serverless architecture, you gain a resilient processing pipeline that scales automatically from 0 to 10,000 images per minute with zero maintenance overhead and virtually zero idle costs.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from Amazon VPCs and your on-premises networks without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this comprehensive hands-on workshop, you will learn how to design, configure, and validate VPC endpoints that allow hybrid cloud workloads to interact with AWS services with enterprise-grade isolation and zero internet egress dependencies.
You will implement and evaluate two distinct types of VPC endpoints for Amazon S3:
Gateway VPC Endpoint: Directs traffic from subnets to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB via private AWS internal routing. Traffic is routed using VPC Route Table prefix lists at zero additional service cost. Interface VPC Endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink): Provisions elastic network interfaces (ENIs) with private IP addresses inside your VPC subnets, enabling seamless, secure access from on-premises datacenters over VPN or AWS Direct Connect. title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Thoughts, Reflections & Constructive Feedback The 12-week journey with the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) bootcamp has been one of the most rewarding and formative experiences of my academic life. Beyond the technical knowledge gained, this program transformed how I approach engineering problems, collaborate with peers, and navigate real-world cloud challenges.
Below are my honest reflections and constructive recommendations for future cohort iterations:
Detailed Program Evaluation 1. Learning Environment & Culture Impression: The learning atmosphere is exceptionally welcoming, energetic, and supportive. From day one, senior mentors and team coordinators treated interns as colleagues rather than mere students. Positive Highlight: The active discussion channels on Slack/Facebook Group provided rapid assistance whenever someone ran into tricky IAM permissions or VPC peering bugs, even late in the evening. Suggestion: It would be fantastic to incorporate more informal team bonding activities or virtual coffee chats to foster even deeper connections among participants across different university campuses. 2. Quality of Mentorship & Leadership Guidance Impression: The mentors are deeply knowledgeable, patient, and inspiring. The “Teach to Fish” Philosophy: Instead of simply handing out quick code snippets to fix our errors, mentors consistently asked probing questions (e.g., “What does CloudWatch Logs show? What is the HTTP status code returning?”), training us to develop autonomous troubleshooting reflexes. Suggestion: Scheduling bi-weekly 1-on-1 progress check-ins with mentors would be immensely valuable for interns to receive targeted individual feedback on personal career roadmaps. 3. Alignment with University Curriculum & Industry Demands Impression: The curriculum serves as the perfect bridge between university computer science foundations (Operating Systems, Computer Networks, Database Systems) and modern industrial cloud engineering. Value: Theoretical knowledge of routing protocols or relational schemas came alive when we actually configured Route Tables, NAT Gateways, and Multi-AZ RDS clusters in live AWS production environments. 4. Growth in Soft Skills & Engineering Maturity Key Gains: In addition to technical proficiency, the mandatory requirements to write weekly worklogs, publish community blogs, and present capstone workshops drastically enhanced my technical writing, storytelling, and public speaking abilities. Key Questions & Retrospective Thoughts What was the most satisfying moment during your internship? The most thrilling milestone was the moment my automated CI/CD pipeline triggered by a Git push successfully tested, built, and deployed the entire multi-region architecture without a single manual console click. Seeing theory transform into working, highly available cloud infrastructure was unforgettable.
What could the program improve for upcoming cohorts? Curated Lab Budget Credits: Providing dedicated AWS credit vouchers or sandbox accounts with pre-allocated budgets would give students even greater peace of mind to experiment boldly with heavier services like Amazon OpenSearch or Amazon EKS without worrying about personal credit card charges. Architecture Whiteboard Challenges: Adding interactive whiteboard architecture design sessions in small teams would sharpen rapid system design interview skills. Would you recommend this program to fellow university students? Absolutely 100% yes. I have already encouraged several promising juniors in my university’s IT faculty to apply for upcoming cohorts. The First Cloud AI Journey provides practical, resume-defining engineering skills that simply cannot be acquired through textbooks alone.
Sincere Words of Appreciation I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to the entire First Cloud AI Journey leadership team, AWS Vietnam mentors, and my wonderful fellow interns. Thank you for creating an extraordinary learning platform, for your selfless guidance, and for empowering young students to step boldly into the cloud computing era!
